scope: Collaborative examples; no universal targets or clinical mandates. Differential assessment, safety, medical needs, age and consent govern selection.

ideas.title: Test a frightening prediction
ideas.try: Choose one manageable prediction such as 'I will lose control in the meeting.' Write what happened after the meeting, including surprises.
ideas.measure: Compare prediction with observation, not simply whether anxiety dropped.

ideas.title: Reduce avoidable sensory load
ideas.try: Try turning off unneeded alerts, moving to a quieter seat, or asking for written directions for two work periods.
ideas.measure: Track participation and mental effort with and without the change.

ideas.title: Make expectations predictable
ideas.try: Ask for an agenda, a specific starting time, or clear next steps before one stressful event.
ideas.measure: Record whether the information improved access and decision-making.

ideas.title: Make one choice without extra reassurance
ideas.try: Choose a low-stakes decision, decide with the available information, and return to a meaningful task without repeated checking.
ideas.measure: Notice extra reassurance attempts and whether the action was completed.

ideas.title: Build a reset routine
ideas.try: Try a chosen rest, food, movement, or sensory break before a difficult task on three occasions.
ideas.measure: Compare ability to participate and personal comfort afterward.

ideas.title: Share a useful support request
ideas.try: Ask one person for concrete help, such as a brief check-in or a written summary, without asking them to guarantee an outcome.
ideas.measure: Track whether the specific support was available and helpful.

ideas.title: Act on what matters while uncertain
ideas.try: Choose one small valued action and try it even if worry is still present, without pressuring yourself to feel calm first.
ideas.measure: Count meaningful actions and note how freely you could choose.

ideas.title: Notice worry versus useful planning
ideas.try: For one worry, identify what is actionable today and what has no useful next step. Spend ten minutes on the actionable part and move on.
ideas.measure: Note decisions made and time lost to looping.

ideas.title: Adjust an unreasonable demand
ideas.try: Identify one unnecessary task step, unclear expectation, or inaccessible deadline and negotiate a feasible alternative.
ideas.measure: Track task completion, effort, and whether the adjustment was accepted.

ideas.title: Explore a safe avoided situation
ideas.try: With a clinician when exposure is indicated, select a small step toward a genuinely safe activity and repeat it on two occasions.
ideas.measure: Track avoidance, participation, and learning rather than forced calm.

ideas.title: Ask for accompaniment, not rescue
ideas.try: Try having a trusted person join the first attempt at a difficult but safe activity, with an agreed plan to preserve your choice.
ideas.measure: Record what support enabled and whether it reinforced independence or dependence.

ideas.title: Protect choice and limits
ideas.try: Name one demand you can decline or renegotiate. Practice a direct response once without supplying a long justification.
ideas.measure: Notice whether your boundary was honored and how it affected functioning.

ideas.title: Lower the barrier to starting
ideas.try: Put needed materials within reach or use a ready-to-go activity kit for one enjoyable task this week.
ideas.measure: Note whether access improved and whether effort became more manageable.

ideas.title: Respond to one self-critical story
ideas.try: Write down a harsh conclusion after a setback and identify one equally plausible, less condemning account.
ideas.measure: Track willingness to try the next step afterward.

ideas.title: Choose connection on your terms
ideas.try: Ask a supportive person for a short shared activity instead of an open-ended social obligation.
ideas.measure: Notice connection quality and energy cost.

ideas.title: Protect one personally meaningful role
ideas.try: Pick a small step toward being the friend, artist, parent, or community member you want to be.
ideas.measure: Record meaningful participation, not just mood improvement.

ideas.title: Protect routine from avoidable disruption
ideas.try: With the care team, reduce one source of unnecessary sleep or schedule disruption and review whether the adjustment works.
ideas.measure: Track feasible routine consistency and next-day functioning.

ideas.title: Name the personal warning pattern
ideas.try: Describe two changes that have preceded episodes, using your history rather than generic checklists.
ideas.measure: Check whether you can recognize the pattern and know who to contact.

ideas.title: Share the early-response plan
ideas.try: With consent, agree on one way a trusted supporter can raise a concern and one step the client can choose next.
ideas.measure: Review clarity, acceptability, and how promptly support can be accessed.

ideas.title: Preserve meaningful activities safely
ideas.try: Choose a valued routine that can remain accessible during treatment changes, adjusting the intensity with the care team.
ideas.measure: Track participation and stability rather than productivity alone.

ideas.title: Separate predictions from facts
ideas.try: For a recurring worry, write the specific feared outcome, available evidence, and what remains unknown. Revisit after one real opportunity.
ideas.measure: Count decisions or actions completed without resolving all uncertainty.

ideas.title: Ask for clearer information
ideas.try: Replace one vague responsibility with a written next step, named contact, or predictable deadline.
ideas.measure: Track the amount of time spent seeking clarification and task completion.

ideas.title: Delay unnecessary checking
ideas.try: If checking is not needed for safety, agree to postpone one repeated check and return to a valued action.
ideas.measure: Track checking frequency and ability to carry on while unsure.

ideas.title: Schedule practical problem-solving
ideas.try: Set a brief time for one actionable problem; afterward, practice returning attention to the current activity.
ideas.measure: Notice decisions made and time spent revisiting the same issue.

ideas.title: Review the feared meaning of sensations
ideas.try: With your clinician, compare a catastrophic prediction about a familiar panic sensation with what has been observed medically and in practice.
ideas.measure: Track conviction in the prediction and participation.

ideas.title: Create a navigable route
ideas.try: For a safe destination, choose a practical route, clear directions, and an accessible exit without turning the plan into repeated escape checking.
ideas.measure: Track whether access improves and which supports are genuinely needed.

ideas.title: Practice safe interoceptive learning
ideas.try: When medically appropriate and clinician-guided, try a small sensation exercise and review what was predicted versus what happened.
ideas.measure: Record learning and willingness to participate, not just symptom intensity.

ideas.title: Explain the support that helps
ideas.try: Agree on a response a trusted person can offer during panic that avoids excessive reassurance while respecting medical needs.
ideas.measure: Review whether the support maintains choice and activity.

ideas.title: Test the mind-reading story
ideas.try: After a chosen interaction, compare a feared judgment with the actual information available rather than assuming you know what others thought.
ideas.measure: Notice self-criticism and willingness to interact again.

ideas.title: Choose a workable social setting
ideas.try: Try a smaller gathering, a quiet meeting space, or a structured activity that suits your sensory and social needs.
ideas.measure: Compare comfort, participation and authenticity across settings.

ideas.title: Reduce one safety performance
ideas.try: In an agreed, safe conversation, practice speaking without rehearsing every sentence or apologizing automatically.
ideas.measure: Track engagement, predicted outcomes, and the aftermath.

ideas.title: Practice a genuine connection bid
ideas.try: Send a specific invitation or ask a question about an interest you share with someone.
ideas.measure: Notice reciprocity and whether the connection feels worthwhile.

ideas.title: Compare expectation with observation
ideas.try: Before an agreed safe step toward the feared situation, name the predicted consequence; afterward, note what actually occurred.
ideas.measure: Track learning from the attempt, not whether fear vanished.

ideas.title: Make the activity accessible
ideas.try: Separate real sensory, physical or safety barriers from the feared cue and address a concrete access barrier first.
ideas.measure: Track whether participation becomes possible without invalidating the fear.

ideas.title: Build a collaborative approach ladder
ideas.try: With an appropriate clinician, choose two manageable steps toward a safe valued activity, allowing assent and pacing.
ideas.measure: Record approach attempts and functional access.

ideas.title: Plan supported participation
ideas.try: Ask a caregiver or trusted companion to support a first step without forcing, shaming, or taking over.
ideas.measure: Track the person's choice, participation and trust.

ideas.title: Label the uncertainty loop
ideas.try: During an agreed ERP plan, notice when a thought asks for impossible certainty rather than a genuinely new safety fact.
ideas.measure: Track time spent in mental reviewing and progress with valued actions.

ideas.title: Reduce ritual invitations in routines
ideas.try: With the person and clinician, change one predictable family or setting cue that unnecessarily prompts reassurance or accommodation.
ideas.measure: Track ritual-support requests and respectful alternative responses.

ideas.title: Practice response prevention
ideas.try: With an ERP clinician, choose a manageable exposure and practice not doing the agreed overt or mental ritual while continuing the valued task.
ideas.measure: Track response prevention and functional participation.

ideas.title: Rehearse a supportive, non-reassuring reply
ideas.try: Choose one brief validating answer to a repeated OCD reassurance request and practice it consistently by agreement.
ideas.measure: Track accommodation, agency and quality of support.

ideas.title: Notice appearance certainty-seeking
ideas.try: Identify a specific appearance judgment and the checking or comparison cycle that follows, without arguing about whether the judgment is true.
ideas.measure: Track time spent pursuing certainty and activities missed.

ideas.title: Reduce unnecessary checking triggers
ideas.try: Try moving a magnifying mirror or social-media comparison cue out of one daily routine with agreement.
ideas.measure: Notice time recovered and participation, not appearance ratings.

ideas.title: Return to an avoided activity
ideas.try: With suitable clinical support, practice one chosen activity while reducing an agreed checking or concealment ritual.
ideas.measure: Track engagement and safety behaviors.

ideas.title: Ask for functional rather than appearance feedback
ideas.try: Agree with a supporter on replies that emphasize needs, choice and activity rather than repeated attractiveness reassurance.
ideas.measure: Track usefulness and checking requests.

ideas.title: Make one setting genuinely safer
ideas.try: Identify a current environmental cue that creates an avoidable access or safety problem and change it where possible.
ideas.measure: Track felt safety, choice and participation after the change.

ideas.title: Distinguish now from then
ideas.try: With clinician support, identify one concrete piece of present-day information that can help orient during a trauma reminder.
ideas.measure: Track the ability to regain orientation and make a choice.

ideas.title: Return to one safe valued activity
ideas.try: Collaboratively plan a tolerable return to an activity that is currently safe but restricted by reminders.
ideas.measure: Track choice, participation and avoidance without forced exposure.

ideas.title: Agree on trauma-informed support
ideas.try: Tell a trusted person one way to offer options, consent and predictability when reminders arise.
ideas.measure: Track whether support respects boundaries and aids recovery.

ideas.title: Reconsider an impossible standard
ideas.try: Name one expectation that suited the previous situation but no longer fits. Choose a workable temporary alternative.
ideas.measure: Review strain and actual follow-through.

ideas.title: Change the daily setup
ideas.try: Move a task, share one responsibility or reduce an unnecessary deadline conflict while adapting to the transition.
ideas.measure: Track hours or effort recovered and essential tasks completed.

ideas.title: Make support specific
ideas.try: Ask someone for one defined kind of help this week instead of a vague offer to 'be available.'
ideas.measure: Notice whether help arrives and preserves agency.

ideas.title: Keep one continuity ritual
ideas.try: Choose an activity that connects past values with the new life situation and try it once this week.
ideas.measure: Rate its personal meaning and practical feasibility.

ideas.title: Allow mixed feelings without judgment
ideas.try: When grief and enjoyment occur together, try naming both experiences without treating one as a betrayal of the other.
ideas.measure: Notice freedom to participate in the moment.

ideas.title: Make space for reminders and rest
ideas.try: Choose when and where to engage with belongings or memories, including the option to pause, instead of reacting to every cue.
ideas.measure: Track sense of choice and daily functioning.

ideas.title: Ask for the kind of presence you want
ideas.try: Tell one supporter whether you want company, practical assistance or time to talk about the person.
ideas.measure: Notice support fit and connection.

ideas.title: Carry a chosen connection forward
ideas.try: Try a remembrance activity that fits your own beliefs and relationships rather than a prescribed stage of grief.
ideas.measure: Reflect on meaning and whether it remains your choice.

ideas.title: Name experiences without blame
ideas.try: With appropriate clinical support, replace a self-critical explanation for a memory gap with a descriptive account of what is known and unknown.
ideas.measure: Track shame, cooperation and ability to plan safely.

ideas.title: Create consistent orientation cues
ideas.try: Try a visible date board, predictable room setup or quiet grounding location chosen by the person.
ideas.measure: Notice orientation and access without imposing sensory input.

ideas.title: Agree on consent-respecting assistance
ideas.try: Ask a trusted person to use one chosen orientation prompt and to stop if it becomes intrusive.
ideas.measure: Track felt control, distress and usefulness.

ideas.title: Keep continuity around valued tasks
ideas.try: Use a consensual note or reminder for one personally meaningful daily task and review whether it supports cooperation.
ideas.measure: Track continuity, autonomy and conflict.

ideas.title: Hold more than one interpretation
ideas.try: After a manageable relational misunderstanding, name two possible explanations before drawing a conclusion.
ideas.measure: Notice urges to act immediately and whether communication improves.

ideas.title: Create a predictable pause option
ideas.try: Agree with a partner on a clear break-and-return routine before a difficult discussion, without using silence as punishment.
ideas.measure: Track whether breaks protect safety and lead to return.

ideas.title: Practice one alternative to escalation
ideas.try: Rehearse a preferred distress-tolerance or direct-request step when emotions are moderate, then review actual use.
ideas.measure: Track safety, agency and communication.

ideas.title: Ask directly rather than test
ideas.try: Try one clear request for contact, information or boundaries without withdrawing or escalating as an indirect signal.
ideas.measure: Notice whether the request is understood and respected.

ideas.title: Check the familiar relationship story
ideas.try: Identify an assumption about another person's intention and ask what current evidence does or does not support it.
ideas.measure: Track flexibility and chosen responses.

ideas.title: Change a recurring conflict setup
ideas.try: Move an important conversation out of a rushed or public setting and agree on a manageable time.
ideas.measure: Track whether choice and mutual understanding improve.

ideas.title: Practice a boundary without attacking
ideas.try: State one preference or limit clearly while making room for the other person's response and safety.
ideas.measure: Notice follow-through and relational impact.

ideas.title: Choose a response that fits identity
ideas.try: Before one difficult interaction, identify the kind of person you want to be and one workable behavior that expresses that value.
ideas.measure: Track value-consistent actions rather than conflict avoidance.

ideas.title: Explore distress without arguing over beliefs
ideas.try: With the clinician, focus on what an experience means to the person and what affects distress, while keeping dialogue collaborative.
ideas.measure: Track distress and ability to do chosen activities.

ideas.title: Reduce avoidable stressors
ideas.try: Try one practical adjustment such as quieter space, predictable instructions or reduced task load while maintaining needed care.
ideas.measure: Track participation, stress and support availability.

ideas.title: Clarify a recovery support plan
ideas.try: Choose one trusted contact and an agreed way to ask for help when experiences become harder to manage.
ideas.measure: Track access to support and self-defined recovery.

ideas.title: Protect a chosen role
ideas.try: Select a personally important activity and identify the accommodations needed to take part safely.
ideas.measure: Track satisfaction, choice and participation.

ideas.title: Replace moral judgments with task information
ideas.try: After a delayed task, identify whether the obstacle was starting, remembering, sequencing or accessing materials instead of calling it laziness.
ideas.measure: Track which change improves follow-through.

ideas.title: Put the next step where it happens
ideas.try: Place a single visual cue and required materials at the real starting location for one task.
ideas.measure: Track time to start and prompts needed.

ideas.title: Try a two-minute entry step
ideas.try: For one chosen task, commit only to opening the file, placing the first item or completing another visible beginning.
ideas.measure: Track starts versus opportunities, with supports.

ideas.title: Request accountability that helps
ideas.try: Ask a supportive person for a brief body-double session or neutral check-in without criticism.
ideas.measure: Track task completion and whether support feels acceptable.

ideas.title: Validate the communication mismatch
ideas.try: When a social task goes poorly, compare interpretations such as lack of clarity, different expectations or sensory overload rather than assuming deficient motivation.
ideas.measure: Track whether needs are understood.

ideas.title: Change the sensory and instruction load
ideas.try: Offer a quiet option, visual schedule or written sequence chosen with the autistic person.
ideas.measure: Track access, overload and decision-making.

ideas.title: Make refusal a real choice
ideas.try: Build yes, no, not now and another option into one everyday decision using the person's communication mode.
ideas.measure: Track whether choices are respected.

ideas.title: Choose goals beyond normalization
ideas.try: Ask what matters to the person, including belonging, autonomy, interests and support, without targeting harmless autistic traits.
ideas.measure: Track personally meaningful participation and agency.

ideas.title: Make information understandable
ideas.try: Try explaining one real choice with short language, images and time to respond, then check comprehension without leading.
ideas.measure: Notice whether the person can express their actual preference.

ideas.title: Remove a preventable access barrier
ideas.try: Change one environment, instruction or communication format that stops participation in a chosen activity.
ideas.measure: Track access and required support.

ideas.title: Honor refusal and consent
ideas.try: Offer a genuine no or later option in a routine choice, using supported communication as needed.
ideas.measure: Track opportunities offered and choices honored.

ideas.title: Build on existing strengths
ideas.try: Choose one preferred activity and identify the minimum practical assistance required to participate meaningfully.
ideas.measure: Track participation and autonomy, not independence for its own sake.

ideas.title: Look for the unmet function
ideas.try: In one repeated conflict, consider whether unclear directions, a difficult task, sensory load or relational stress precede escalation.
ideas.measure: Compare contexts and support responses without labeling intent.

ideas.title: Prevent a predictable conflict
ideas.try: Shorten an unclear instruction, prepare materials or change a transition routine with the young person's input.
ideas.measure: Track conflict and task access.

ideas.title: Practice a replacement request
ideas.try: During a calm moment, teach and rehearse a clear break, help or return request for one common trigger.
ideas.measure: Record use and adult follow-through.

ideas.title: Coordinate adult responses
ideas.try: Agree among caregivers on one calm response to the child's replacement request and avoid escalating power struggles.
ideas.measure: Track consistency and felt safety.

ideas.title: Spot the interpretation before escalation
ideas.try: After a low-stakes frustration, name an assumption about intent and consider another explanation before responding.
ideas.measure: Track flexibility and the chosen next action.

ideas.title: Build a safe pause point
ideas.try: Agree on an exit to a quiet space or a pause-and-return arrangement that does not trap others in conflict.
ideas.measure: Track safer exits and return to discussion.

ideas.title: Rehearse a safer first response
ideas.try: Practice a concrete step such as stepping away, asking for help or stating a boundary during two calm moments.
ideas.measure: Track use during real early-warning opportunities.

ideas.title: Repair without demanding forgiveness
ideas.try: After a manageable conflict, acknowledge the impact and offer a specific corrective action while respecting the other person's choice.
ideas.measure: Track safety and actual follow-through.

ideas.title: Explore the trade-off without shame
ideas.try: Write down one reason for current substance use and one personally important cost or concern, then choose what to examine next.
ideas.measure: Track clarity and readiness for change, not compliance.

ideas.title: Adjust one high-risk context
ideas.try: With the treatment team, identify a practical environment change that reduces exposure to an unwanted trigger or makes support easier to reach.
ideas.measure: Track harm events and feasibility.

ideas.title: Identify low-barrier help
ideas.try: Find one person or service the client is willing and able to contact when support is needed; rehearse how to reach them.
ideas.measure: Track support access and usefulness.

ideas.title: Set a personally meaningful change goal
ideas.try: Choose one collaborative, clinically appropriate next step toward reducing harm or meeting the client's stated recovery goal.
ideas.measure: Track relevant function and harms without punishment.

ideas.title: Notice a recovery-blocking rule
ideas.try: With the eating-disorder team, identify one rigid rule interfering with specialist-agreed care and review its role without negotiating medical necessity.
ideas.measure: Track engagement with team-approved care.

ideas.title: Reduce access barriers to treatment
ideas.try: With the care team, arrange privacy, transportation, predictable appointments or other practical access needs.
ideas.measure: Track attendance and barriers addressed.

ideas.title: Specify helpful meal support
ideas.try: Ask the specialist team and trusted supporters to agree on one respectful, non-coercive form of assistance.
ideas.measure: Track participation, safety and experienced support.

ideas.title: Preserve identity beyond symptoms
ideas.try: Choose a valued relationship, interest or role that can be supported during treatment without compromising medical care.
ideas.measure: Track meaningful participation.

ideas.title: Examine shame without punitive tracking
ideas.try: With the clinician, identify a harsh conclusion after an episode and practice a compassionate next step toward the agreed recovery plan.
ideas.measure: Track return to treatment, not self-punishment.

ideas.title: Improve access to approved support
ideas.try: Arrange private check-ins, predictable treatment contact or practical assistance for the care plan.
ideas.measure: Track barriers and adherence to team-agreed care.

ideas.title: Plan one supportive response
ideas.try: Agree on how a trusted person can respond helpfully to distress without policing, shaming or encouraging rituals.
ideas.measure: Track perceived support and clinical participation.

ideas.title: Reclaim an activity unrelated to food or weight
ideas.try: Choose one meaningful activity that can be sustained safely alongside eating-disorder treatment.
ideas.measure: Track access, enjoyment and personal connection.

ideas.title: Name the actual barrier
ideas.try: With appropriate assessment, distinguish sensory sensitivity, fear of aversive consequences and limited interest rather than assuming defiance.
ideas.measure: Track whether support matches the identified need.

ideas.title: Make eating access more predictable
ideas.try: With specialist guidance, change one sensory or scheduling barrier, such as seating, noise or a clear menu preview.
ideas.measure: Track safe participation and tolerability.

ideas.title: Create a usable needs signal
ideas.try: Agree on a simple way to ask for a pause, help or a suitable option during eating-related activities.
ideas.measure: Track whether needs are recognized and honored.

ideas.title: Protect dignity and choice
ideas.try: Include the person in decisions about the pace and form of team-approved feeding practices rather than requiring public performance.
ideas.measure: Track agency and participation.

ideas.title: Reduce sleep-performance pressure
ideas.try: With appropriate CBT-I guidance, notice one 'I must sleep now' rule and choose a less adversarial response to wakefulness.
ideas.measure: Track sleep-related distress and daytime function.

ideas.title: Change one practical sleep barrier
ideas.try: Adjust a manageable source of light, noise or interruptions consistent with medical and caregiving needs.
ideas.measure: Track comfort and next-day functioning.

ideas.title: Try a feasible wake routine
ideas.try: With clinician input where indicated, choose one consistent morning step that fits real-life responsibilities.
ideas.measure: Track feasibility and daytime function.

ideas.title: Negotiate shared sleep needs
ideas.try: Ask a household member for one concrete change that makes rest more accessible while respecting everyone's needs.
ideas.measure: Review whether the accommodation worked.

ideas.title: Balance uncertainty with medical care
ideas.try: Identify one catastrophic interpretation of a familiar symptom, then discuss alternative explanations and appropriate follow-up with the clinician.
ideas.measure: Track functional impact without dismissing symptoms.

ideas.title: Make valued activity accessible
ideas.try: Modify pacing, location or physical setup for one important activity while following appropriate medical advice.
ideas.measure: Track participation and after-effects.

ideas.title: Reduce unnecessary reassurance loops
ideas.try: Only after determining what monitoring is medically indicated, try one agreed reduction in repetitive non-indicated checking.
ideas.measure: Track checking and meaningful activity.

ideas.title: Agree on consistent medical communication
ideas.try: Choose one appropriate contact plan with the medical team to avoid fragmented, confusing advice.
ideas.measure: Track clarity and care access.

ideas.title: Notice all-or-nothing activity judgments
ideas.try: After a difficult day, test whether a small adapted version of a valued activity can still count as meaningful participation.
ideas.measure: Track choice and impact rather than pain elimination.

ideas.title: Adapt the task setup
ideas.try: Try ergonomic, sensory or scheduling supports for a valued activity, guided by clinical and medical advice as appropriate.
ideas.measure: Track ability to participate and flare effects.

ideas.title: Try sustainable pacing
ideas.try: Choose a manageable amount of a meaningful activity and review after-effects before increasing it.
ideas.measure: Track sustainable participation across days.

ideas.title: Make assistance specific
ideas.try: Ask a support person for help with one painful or exhausting step while keeping desired control over the task.
ideas.measure: Track autonomy, participation and support fit.

ideas.title: Interpret distress as information
ideas.try: When a familiar routine fails, consider confusion, pain, noise or unmet needs rather than treating the response as willful behavior.
ideas.measure: Track which context change helps.

ideas.title: Simplify a familiar setting
ideas.try: Try consistent object placement, a single visual cue, or reduced distraction for one meaningful routine.
ideas.measure: Track ease, enjoyment and safety.

ideas.title: Offer supported choices
ideas.try: Present one or two meaningful, understandable options, allowing time and a genuine decline.
ideas.measure: Track preferences communicated and honored.

ideas.title: Keep a valued identity visible
ideas.try: With the person and caregivers, choose a familiar hobby or role and adapt its demands so participation remains possible.
ideas.measure: Track engagement and connection.
